payloads.replacement:
A **relation**, $\mathcal{R}$, from set $X$ to set $Y$ is a collection of ordered pairs $(x,y)$, where $x$ comes from $X$ and $y$ comes from $Y$.

We say $\mathcal{R}$ **‘maps’** elements of $X$ to elements of $Y$: $\mathcal{R}:x\mapsto y$.

In set notation, $X$ is the entire set and $x$ is an individual element of $X$.
Real relations matter in this course because we can graph them on the Cartesian plane and easily see their behaviour and properties.
A **function** $f$ is a relation in which each $x$-value has only one $y$-value (only one arrow leaves each $x$-value).

Think of a function as a **function machine**: it takes an input number, applies a rule, then gives an output number.

$x$ is the **input** and $y$ is the **output**.

For a function, every input has at most one output.

An example is the linear function $y=2x+3$.

**For a function** $y=f(x)$

$f(a)$ means find the $y$ coordinate when $x=a$.

$f(x)=c$ means find every $x$ coordinate where $y=c$ (there may be none, one or several).

For $y=f(x)$:

$f(0)$ is the $y$-coordinate of the **$y$-intercept**.

A **zero** of the function is an $x$ value where $f(x)=0$ (the $x$-coordinate of an **$x$-intercept**).

A function can have many zeroes but at most one $f(0)$.

The **domain** of a function is the set of all inputs ($x$-values) the function accepts.
We can write a domain as an interval, and visualise it as a shadow of the graph on the $x$-axis.

A function's **natural domain** is the set of all real $x$-values for which the rule gives a real $y$-value.

Many functions have no restriction on their domain, but some do.

When finding the natural domain, remember:

- **Denominators cannot be zero.**
- **The expression inside a square root must be non-negative.**

The **natural range** is the set of all outputs the function takes over its natural domain.

It is most easily found by sketching the graph. To find it algebraically, use:

$$\sqrt{\text{expression}}\ge 0,\qquad (\text{expression})^2\ge 0,\qquad \frac{1}{\text{expression}}\ne 0$$
